stories.headline: US midterm votes are cast, but control of Congress is still unknown
stories.question: Who controls the US Congress now, and what does it mean for Trump?
stories.dek: Americans voted on 3 November 2026, but no results were in when we researched this. Republicans hold 53 of 100 Senate seats for now. The result decides whether Trump's veto becomes his main tool.

so_far.text: The US held its midterm elections on 3 November 2026. Midterms come halfway through a president's four-year term, and many see this one as a referendum on President Donald Trump. Voters chose members of both the House and the Senate. Republicans now hold 53 of the 100 Senate seats. They need only 50 to keep control, because Vice President JD Vance breaks ties. Before voting, forecasters favoured Democrats to win the House. Trump threatened to veto everything if Democrats win Congress.

what_happened.text: Americans voted on 3 November 2026. When this edition was researched, no results or race calls were available. Searches returned only pre-election material. So it is not yet known who will control the House or the Senate. In the Senate, Fox News rated six races as toss-ups. Five are seats Republicans are defending: Alaska, Iowa, Maine, South Carolina and Texas. One, Michigan, is defended by Democrats. Fox News rated Ohio as leaning Democratic and Kansas as leaning Republican. Voters also chose 36 governors and decided 145 statewide ballot measures, including California's Prop 40 billionaire tax.

The party with a majority in a chamber decides which bills get a vote there.
In the Senate, Republicans keep control with 50 seats, because Vice President JD Vance breaks ties.
If Democrats win both chambers, they can send Trump bills; he says he would veto everything.

lesson.concept: How a US president's veto and its override work
lesson.big_idea: A US law needs the House, the Senate and the president. The president can say no with a veto. Congress can overrule that veto only if two-thirds of both chambers agree.

steps.title: Both chambers must pass it
steps.text: A bill becomes law only after the House and the Senate (100 members) pass the same text. Each needs a majority, meaning more than half of those voting.

steps.title: Majority control sets the agenda
steps.text: The party with more than half the seats in a chamber decides which bills get a vote there. In the Senate, 50 seats is enough for Republicans, because Vice President JD Vance breaks ties.

steps.title: The president signs or vetoes
steps.text: A passed bill goes to the president. If he signs it, it becomes law. If he vetoes it, meaning he rejects it, it goes back to Congress. Trump has threatened to veto everything from a Democratic Congress.

steps.title: Override needs two-thirds of both
steps.text: Congress can overrule a veto only if two-thirds of both chambers vote to pass the bill again. A simple majority is not enough, and failing in either chamber means the veto stands.

steps.title: Count the switchers needed
steps.text: To judge whether a veto is safe, count how many members of the president's own party must switch sides. The bigger that gap, the safer the veto.

stories.headline: Indian sailor killed as aerial object hits ship off Oman
stories.question: How did an Indian sailor die near Oman, and are Indian seafarers safe?
stories.dek: On 2 November, an unidentified object from the air hit the Indian-flagged MSV Al Jusufi off Oman and killed a sailor from Gujarat. India's rules lower the risk at sea, but they cannot remove it.

so_far.text: A war in West Asia began on 28 February 2026. Soon after, ships in the Gulf region started coming under attack. By early March, 37 Indian-flagged ships with 1,109 sailors were stuck in the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. By 16 July, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) had counted 57 confirmed incidents in the region. Attacks on 11 and 14 July killed Indian engineers. India's shipping regulator, the Directorate General of Shipping, then acted. On 15 July it told ship owners, managers and recruiters not to put Indian seafarers on ships crossing the Strait of Hormuz until further notice.

what_happened.text: On the evening of Monday 2 November, an unidentified aerial object hit the Indian-flagged vessel MSV Al Jusufi. The ship was near Limah, in Oman's Musandam Governorate, with 14 crew aboard. One Indian seafarer, a man from Gujarat, was killed. The other 13 were rescued. One report says Oman's coast guard rescued them. India's external affairs ministry (MEA) confirmed the death and called for immediate de-escalation. The Indian embassy in Muscat is arranging to bring the survivors and the body home. It is not yet known who launched the object.

steps.text: Musandam sits on the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that every ship entering or leaving the Gulf must use.
The danger there is real. By 16 July, the IMO had counted 57 confirmed incidents and 18 seafarer deaths in the Gulf region.
India cannot stop the attacks. So its regulator lowers the danger by keeping Indian crews off ships crossing Hormuz.
That order lowers the risk but cannot remove it. Indian-flagged vessels still sail near the strait, and Al Jusufi was one of them.
Once a ship is hit, the crew's survival depends on a fast rescue nearby, then help from the embassy, then diplomacy to calm the war.

lesson.concept: How India protects its sailors in a war zone
lesson.big_idea: India cannot stop attacks at sea. So it protects sailors in layers: keep them out of the worst waters, give ships an emergency line, then rely on nearby rescue, the embassy and diplomacy.

steps.title: A ship's flag sets rules
steps.text: Every ship is registered to a country, called its flag. An Indian-flagged ship, like MSV Al Jusufi, follows Indian rules. India's shipping regulator, the Directorate General of Shipping, oversees its safety.

steps.title: Layer one: avoid the danger
steps.text: The regulator can tell owners, managers and recruiters where Indian crews may work. Since 15 July, it has said no Indian seafarers should be on ships crossing Hormuz until further notice.

steps.title: Layer two: an emergency line
steps.text: If a ship is attacked, its master (the captain) is told to contact the DGMA communication centre or IFC-IOR. One report says the regulator works with the Indian Navy and the MEA.

steps.title: Layer three: rescue nearby
steps.text: Help must come from whoever is closest. These attacks happen far from India, so a local coast guard may reach survivors first. Off Oman, one report says Oman's coast guard rescued 13 crew.

steps.title: Layer four: embassy and diplomacy
steps.text: After the rescue, India's embassy brings the survivors and the dead home. The MEA also calls for de-escalation, which tries to reduce the attacks themselves.

The embassy in Muscat is arranging their return. But one sailor from Gujarat still died. The MEA now counts 15 seafarers among the 23 Indians killed in this conflict.

practice.q: Imagine a recruiter in Mumbai offers an Indian engineer a job on a tanker crossing Hormuz. Which layer applies, and what should happen?
practice.answer: Layer one, avoiding the danger, applies. The 15 July order tells recruiters not to deploy Indian seafarers on ships crossing Hormuz until further notice. So the recruiter should not place him on that tanker. If the order is lifted later and the tanker is attacked, layer two applies: the master uses the emergency line.

stories.headline: Why Indians are buying the least gold since 2020
stories.question: Why are Indians buying the least gold in six years, right before Diwali?
stories.dek: Gold costs so much that the same budget now buys fewer grams, and rural incomes are squeezed. The World Gold Council expects 2026 demand to be the lowest since 2020.

so_far.text: Indian families buy gold as jewellery and as savings, often for festivals and weddings. Rural areas make up over half of India's gold demand. Prices have kept rising. At Dhanteras 2025, 24-carat gold hit a then-record ₹1,30,874 per 10 grams. In July–September 2025, demand fell 16% by weight, yet its rupee value rose 23%. In April–June 2026, weight fell 6% while value hit a record ₹1.98 lakh crore. Earlier in 2026, the government raised gold import duties.

what_happened.text: On 3 November 2026, the World Gold Council (WGC), an industry body, reported that Indian gold demand fell 29% year-on-year to 162.5 tonnes in July–September. Jewellery demand fell 20% and investment demand fell 40%, said Sachin Jain, the WGC's India CEO. The WGC now expects 2026 demand of about 650 tonnes. That would be the lowest since 2020, when Covid closed jewellery stores. Official gold imports also fell in the September quarter. Part of the reason is that more gold came in unofficially after the duty rise.

steps.text: Gold is much dearer: 10 grams of 24-carat cost about ₹1,47,660 on 18 October 2026, against ₹1,30,874 at Dhanteras 2025.
Families shop with a fixed rupee budget, so a higher price means fewer grams for the same money.
Budgets are shrinking too: living costs linked to the Iran war rose, and the weakest monsoon in over a decade hurt rural incomes.
Rural areas buy over half of India's gold, so their squeeze pulls national demand down sharply.
Higher import duties raise the official price, and some gold now arrives unofficially, so official imports fall even further.

lesson.concept: Why tonnes fall even when rupee spending holds
lesson.big_idea: Families buy gold with a rupee budget. Divide the budget by the price and you get the grams. When prices rise or budgets shrink, the grams, and so the tonnes, fall.

steps.title: You shop with a budget
steps.text: Most families first decide how many rupees to spend on gold, not how many grams to buy. The weight is whatever that money buys at the counter.

steps.title: Grams equal budget divided by price
steps.text: To find the weight, divide your budget by the price per gram. If gold costs ₹10,000 a gram and you spend ₹1,00,000, you get 10 grams.

steps.title: Price up, grams down
steps.text: When the price rises, the same budget buys fewer grams. So demand counted in tonnes can fall while rupee spending holds or even hits a record, as in April–June 2026.

steps.title: Smaller budgets cut twice
steps.text: If incomes also fall, the budget shrinks. Now fewer rupees meet a higher price, so the weight falls twice over. Rural families, over half of demand, faced this in 2026.

steps.title: Taxes add to the price
steps.text: An import duty is a tax on gold entering India. A higher duty pushes the counter price up further. The government raised duties earlier in 2026, and some gold began arriving unofficially.

apply.text: That is the 2026 story. Ten grams of 24-carat gold cost about ₹1,47,660 on 18 October, about 13% above the Dhanteras 2025 record of ₹1,30,874. Rural budgets shrank after the weakest monsoon in over a decade. The WGC cites both pressures for the 29% fall in July–September demand, to 162.5 tonnes.

practice.q: Say gold rises from ₹10,000 to ₹15,000 a gram, and a family keeps its ₹3,00,000 budget. How much less gold does it buy?
practice.answer: Before: ₹3,00,000 ÷ ₹10,000 = 30 grams. After: ₹3,00,000 ÷ ₹15,000 = 20 grams. 30 − 20 = 10 grams fewer. 10 ÷ 30 = one-third less gold, for the same rupees spent.

stories.headline: US regulator clears first $40-a-year generic of twice-yearly HIV shot
stories.question: Could a $40-a-year HIV shot finally help end new infections worldwide?
stories.dek: It could help a lot. The shot nearly stopped infections in trials, and a cheap Indian-made copy adds supply. But money, testing and country approvals still decide how many people get it.

so_far.text: WHO says 41 million people live with HIV, and 570,000 died of HIV-related causes last year. PrEP, short for pre-exposure prophylaxis, is medicine that keeps HIV-negative people from getting infected. Gilead makes lenacapavir, a PrEP shot given twice a year. In October 2024 Gilead signed royalty-free licences letting generic makers copy it in 120 countries. In 2025 the US FDA approved it, sold as Yeztugo. Its US list price is $28,218 a year. In September 2025 Unitaid and the Gates Foundation said Indian firms Dr. Reddy's and Hetero would sell it at about $40 a year from 2027.

what_happened.text: On 2 November 2026 the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) gave tentative approval to the first generic version of lenacapavir. It is made by Dr. Reddy's Laboratories, based in India. "Tentative" is the FDA's standard label for a generic while the original is still under patent, so it cannot be sold in the US. The generic will cost $40 per person per year in the 120 low- and middle-income countries covered by Gilead's licence. Unitaid, the Clinton Health Access Initiative (CHAI) and Wits RHI backed the work. First supplies are expected in countries by the end of 2026, with wider availability in 2027.

steps.text: Lenacapavir needs just two shots a year, and in two large trials it nearly eliminated new infections.
Until now Gilead was the only supplier, and demand in poorer countries was bigger than supply.
A licensed generic adds a second source, at $40 a year, the same price as daily PrEP pills.
Cheaper doses let the same aid budget protect far more people at risk of HIV.
But buyers still need funding, an HIV test before every shot, and approval in each country.

lesson.concept: How a voluntary licence makes a patented medicine cheap
lesson.big_idea: A patent makes one company the only seller. A voluntary licence lets other makers copy the drug in named countries. Competition pushes the price down, so the same money protects far more people.

steps.title: A patent means one seller
steps.text: A patent gives the inventor the sole right to sell a new drug for some years. Until now Gilead was the only supplier of lenacapavir, and demand in poorer countries was bigger than supply.

steps.title: A licence lets others copy
steps.text: A voluntary licence is permission the patent holder chooses to give. Gilead's licences are royalty-free, meaning no fee per dose. They let licensed makers sell copies in 120 mostly low- and lower-middle-income countries.

steps.title: Copies need a quality check
steps.text: A generic must work like the original. The FDA checks this. While the patent holds, it gives only 'tentative' approval: the copy passes, but cannot be sold in the US.

steps.title: More makers, lower price
steps.text: Generic makers compete with each other and make large batches, so the price falls. Dr. Reddy's generic costs $40 a year in licensed countries. The brand's US list price is $28,218 a year.

steps.title: Price decides how many
steps.text: A health budget is fixed. Divide it by the price per person, and you get how many people it can protect. A lower price means more people from the same money.

example.setup: Say a health programme has $1 million a year to spend on HIV-prevention shots. Let's see how many people it can protect at each price.

lines.note: Yeztugo's US list price, before insurance

example.result: The same $1 million protects about 35 people at the brand's US price, but 25,000 at the generic price. That is why a cheap licensed copy matters as much as the drug itself.

apply.text: So when the FDA tentatively approved Dr. Reddy's copy on 2 November 2026, it added a second source beyond Gilead, at $40 a year. But the budget step still bites. Advocates say about 20 million people need PrEP, and funding to buy the drug for everyone who needs it is still needed.

practice.q: Suppose a different programme has $2 million a year. At the generic price of $40 per person, how many people can it protect?
practice.answer: Divide the budget by the price per person. $2,000,000 ÷ $40 = 50,000 people. Double the money protects double the people. At the brand's US price, the same $2 million would cover only about 70 people.

stories.headline: RBI reopens urban cooperative bank licences after a 22-year freeze
stories.question: Why is RBI letting new urban cooperative banks open after 22 years?
stories.dek: RBI stopped giving out urban cooperative bank licences in 2004 after many new ones failed. The sector is healthier now. RBI is reopening the door, but only for large, clean credit societies.

so_far.text: Urban cooperative banks (UCBs) are banks owned by their members, mostly in towns and cities. In the 1990s RBI gave out many new UCB licences. D. Krishna, former chief of NAFCUB, says many went to people with little cooperative banking experience. Many of those new banks failed, which showed weak governance and weak risk management. So in 2004 RBI stopped issuing licences. The number of UCBs fell from 2,104 in December 2003 to 1,457 in March 2025. On 13 January 2026 RBI released a discussion paper on restarting licensing.

what_happened.text: On 3 November 2026, The Hindu reported that RBI has reopened licensing for urban cooperative banks after 22 years. It also reported that MSCARO and ICAI are building audit guardrails, meaning checks on accounts and governance, for multi-state cooperatives that want to become banks. Before this, RBI published draft on-tap licensing guidelines on 5 August 2026, with public comments due by 5 September 2026. The eligibility rules below come from RBI's January 2026 discussion paper. The August draft may differ.

steps.text: In the 1990s, easy licences put inexperienced people in charge of banks. Many failed, so RBI froze licensing in 2004.
Since then the sector has grown sturdier. Net bad loans fell from 2.7% in 2015 to 0.7%, and the average capital cushion is 18%.
A healthier sector makes letting in new banks less risky. But RBI's proposal opens the door only a little.
Only existing credit societies with ₹300 crore capital, a five-year record and clean books can convert, so very few qualify.
Converting brings a society under RBI's bank rules. As of January 2026, credit society deposits were not covered by DICGC deposit insurance.

lesson.concept: How RBI tests whether a lender is safe enough
lesson.big_idea: A bank lends out other people's money, so RBI checks two things. How thick is its cushion of its own money? And how much of its lending has gone bad? Size and history are checked too.

steps.title: Capital is the cushion
steps.text: A bank lends out depositors' money. Its capital is the owners' own money. When loans go bad, the losses eat into capital first. Depositors stay safe as long as that cushion lasts.

steps.title: CRAR measures the cushion
steps.text: CRAR divides capital by loans, with riskier loans counted more heavily. A higher figure means a thicker cushion. RBI's proposal asks applicants for a CRAR of at least 12%.

steps.title: Net NPA measures the rot
steps.text: An NPA, or non-performing asset, is a loan the borrower has stopped repaying. Take away provisions, the money already set aside for losses, to get net NPA. RBI wants this no higher than 3% of loans.

steps.title: Size and history count too
steps.text: A small lender can have good ratios. So RBI also asks for ₹300 crore of capital as of 31 March of the previous financial year. It also wants a five-year track record and a positive five-year trend.

example.setup: Imagine Sahyog Credit Society wants to become a UCB. It has lent ₹2,000 crore and holds ₹320 crore of its own capital. It has ₹100 crore of bad loans and has set aside ₹60 crore for them.

lines.label: Size test
lines.note: Clears the minimum capital floor

lines.label: CRAR
lines.note: Assume every loan carries full risk. 16% is above the 12% floor.

lines.label: Net bad loans
lines.note: Bad loans minus the money already set aside

lines.label: Net NPA ratio
lines.note: Under the 3% ceiling

lines.label: Verdict
lines.note: It still needs a five-year record and a positive trend

example.result: Sahyog is big enough, its cushion is 16% against a 12% floor, and its net bad loans are 2%, under the 3% ceiling. On the numbers, it can apply.

apply.text: This is why the reopening is so narrow. The ratio tests ask whether a society is safe. The ₹300 crore floor asks whether it is big. Industry executives say only two or three societies pass the size test. D. Krishna proposes tiered capital of ₹25 crore, ₹50 crore and ₹100 crore, and wants medium-sized societies brought under RBI regulation.

practice.q: Imagine a smaller society: ₹1,000 crore lent, ₹150 crore capital, ₹50 crore of bad loans, ₹20 crore set aside. Can it apply?
practice.answer: CRAR: ₹150 crore ÷ ₹1,000 crore = 15%, above 12%, so it passes. Net bad loans: ₹50 crore − ₹20 crore = ₹30 crore. ₹30 crore ÷ ₹1,000 crore = 3%, which is not above 3%, so it passes. Capital: ₹150 crore is below ₹300 crore, so it fails. The society is safe but too small. It would pass Krishna's proposed ₹100 crore multi-state tier.

options: Its capital is below the ₹300 crore minimum
Its CRAR is above the 12% floor
Its net NPA is too low
check.why: The ratios show it is safe. But RBI's proposal also requires ₹300 crore of capital, so it is too small to apply.

takeaways: RBI checks a lender's cushion (CRAR), its bad loans (net NPA), and its size before licensing it.
RBI is reopening UCB licences frozen since 2004, but only for big, clean existing credit societies.
Watch for the final framework and the first licences; no date is known yet.

sections.title: World
sections.gist: Ukraine talks set for Abu Dhabi on 10–11 November; Israel's opposition backs Eisenkot; Spain's transport minister resigns after the train crash.

items.headline: Russia, US and Ukraine to hold talks in Abu Dhabi on 10–11 November
items.text: US envoy Steve Witkoff said talks between Russia, the US and Ukraine will be held in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November. Europe is also preparing for a possible post-war role. From 9 to 22 November, France and the UK will lead about 2,800 troops from 10 European countries in an exercise called Koalicja in southeast Poland. It is the first exercise for the Multinational Force-Ukraine. Western officials stress that any such force would not take part in offensive operations. It would deploy only after the fighting stops. What to watch: whether the Abu Dhabi talks produce any agreement on stopping the fighting.
items.background: The Multinational Force-Ukraine is a planned European force that would go into Ukraine only after the fighting ends.
items.why: The Abu Dhabi talks put all three governments in one place, and their outcome decides whether Europe's planned force is ever used.

items.headline: Bennett's party backs Eisenkot to lead Israel; Netanyahu refuses to go
items.text: Naftali Bennett's B'Yachad faction has thrown its support behind Gadi Eisenkot to form Israel's next government, The Hindu reported on 3 November. Israel's opposition is lining up behind Eisenkot, but Netanyahu refuses to step aside, according to The New Arab. A top Arab-Israeli leader also said the opposition must join forces to remove Netanyahu. The question now is whether the opposition can turn this support into a working government. It is not yet known when, or whether, Eisenkot will be asked to form one.
items.background: After Israel's 27 October election, opposition parties are trying to unite behind one leader, Gadi Eisenkot, to replace Netanyahu.
items.why: Whether the opposition stays united may decide if Netanyahu keeps power or Israel gets a new leader.

items.headline: Spain's transport minister resigns after train crash that killed 69
items.text: Spain's transport minister, Óscar Puente, resigned on 3 November after a train collision south of Madrid killed at least 69 people. Dozens more were injured. Puente also said he will not stand in Spain's upcoming election. His exit makes the crash a political story as well as a safety one. The minister in charge of the country's transport network has now taken responsibility by leaving office. It is not yet known who will replace him.
items.background: At least 69 people died and dozens were hurt when two trains collided south of Madrid, Spain's capital.
items.why: The disaster has now cost Spain's transport minister his job and his place in the coming election.

items.headline: Supermarket freezers across Europe hit by second suspected cyberattack
items.text: Fridges and freezers in supermarkets in several European countries were hit by a new suspected cyberattack, The Guardian reported on 2 November. It is the second such incident. AP also reported that freezers were hit by apparent cyberattacks. A cyberattack here means someone breaking into the computer systems that control the machines. Shop freezers are often linked to networks so staff can watch their temperature remotely. That link is also a door an attacker can use. Officials have not confirmed the attacks, so they are still described as suspected.
items.background: Many shop fridges and freezers are now connected to networks, so they can be controlled and monitored remotely.
items.why: It shows that hackers can target everyday machines that keep food safe, not only office computers.

items.headline: North Korea denies role in record $6.3bn Binance crypto hack
items.text: North Korea's Kim Yo Jong dismissed FBI claims that North Korean hackers stole more than $6 billion from Binance, a large cryptocurrency exchange. She called the US charge a 'provocation', reports on 3 November said. US government agencies and cyber analysts blame Pyongyang for the theft. The BBC puts it at $6.3bn, a record for a crypto heist. Binance has started reopening withdrawals on more networks. Withdrawals let users move their coins out of the exchange. It is not yet known how much of the stolen money can be recovered.
items.background: Binance is one of the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchanges, where people buy, sell and store digital coins.
items.why: Indians who hold crypto on exchanges face the risk that a hack freezes their withdrawals.

items.headline: Foreign Secretary Misri visits Nepal ahead of PM Shah's India trip
items.text: Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri visits Nepal on 4–5 November. The visit prepares for a proposed India trip later in November by Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah. The talks will cover relations between the two countries, connectivity, trade and energy. A foreign secretary is India's top diplomat, below the foreign minister. Visits like this one settle the agenda and the agreements before leaders meet. Dates for Shah's visit have not yet been announced.
items.background: Nepal is a close neighbour linked to India by an open border, trade and energy ties. Balendra Shah is its prime minister.
items.why: Deals on trade, connectivity and energy with Nepal affect cross-border trade and power links with India.

items.headline: US strikes Iran's Qeshm Island hours after Vance praises deal talks
items.text: Late on 2 November, the US launched limited strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island, The Guardian reported. The strikes reportedly targeted surface-to-air missiles being used against US assets. They came hours after Vice-President JD Vance said the US was "feeling pretty good about the prospects" of a deal. They also came on the eve of the US midterm elections. US officials told CBS the strikes were limited and defensive. One US official said Iran had fired at an American aircraft. That account is not independently confirmed.
items.background: The US and Israel have been at war with Iran since strikes began on 28 February 2026.
items.why: No direct effect on India is confirmed yet.

sections.title: India
sections.gist: Navy frees 20 crew from pirates; Visakhapatnam refinery fire contained; SIR row turns to dares to debate; Supreme Court warns states.

items.headline: Fire at HPCL's Visakhapatnam refinery contained, no casualties reported
items.text: A fire broke out late on 2 November in a sulphur pitch storage tank at HPCL's Visakhapatnam refinery in Gajuwaka. An HPCL employee said explosion-like sounds were heard before the fire began. The blaze stayed inside the tank. No casualties were reported. Follow-up reports say the fire was contained and refinery operations were not affected. The exact cause is not yet known. Watch for findings from the company's investigation.
items.background: HPCL, a government-owned oil company, runs a refinery in Visakhapatnam that turns crude oil into fuels.
items.why: With operations reported unaffected, no fuel supply problem has been reported. The cause still matters for refinery safety.

items.headline: Indian Navy frees 20 crew of fishing boat held by pirates
items.text: The Indian Navy rescued all 20 crew of the fishing vessel Azini from armed Somali pirates in the Arabian Sea, reports on 2–3 November said. No one was hurt. The operation lasted more than 48 hours. The Navy sent the warship INS Kolkata, backed by a maritime patrol aircraft. Indian Air Force C-17 transport planes para-dropped Marine Commandos, the Navy's special forces, near the area. The Navy has not yet said what will happen to the pirates.
items.background: Pirates from Somalia attack ships in the Arabian Sea, and the Indian Navy patrols these waters to protect shipping.
items.why: Safe Arabian Sea routes protect India's trade and fuel imports and the many Indian sailors who work at sea.

items.headline: Rahul Gandhi dares Modi to open debate as SIR row grows
items.text: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi dared Prime Minister Narendra Modi to an open debate on 2 November. This came after Home Minister Amit Shah challenged the opposition to discuss SIR in Parliament. SIR is a revision of India's voter lists that opposition parties are protesting. Rahul Gandhi also challenged Modi to debate claims of 'foreign help'. Separately, Congress leader Jairam Ramesh alleged that Shah wants a special session of Parliament to pass delimitation bills. Delimitation means redrawing the boundaries of election seats. Parliament has not been prorogued, meaning its session has not been formally closed. A session that is still open can be recalled quickly.
items.background: Opposition parties accuse the Election Commission of mishandling SIR, a revision of India's voter lists.
items.why: Voter lists decide who can vote, and delimitation decides how seats are drawn; both shape future elections.

items.headline: Supreme Court gives 23 states final chance on prison caste discrimination
items.text: The Supreme Court gave 23 states and union territories a final chance to comply in a case on caste discrimination in prisons, reports on 3 November said. The court warned that it could summon their chief secretaries if they fail. A chief secretary is the top civil servant in a state government. A summons would make them answer to the court in person. The court's next hearing date was not given in the reports.
items.background: The Supreme Court is hearing a case on caste-based discrimination inside India's prisons and has asked states to act.
items.why: It concerns equal treatment of prisoners across most of India's states and union territories.

sections.title: Your money & life
sections.gist: Cyclone Murasu reaches Andhra, Delhi's air turns 'very poor' under GRAP Stage 2, and NEET-UG 2027 may stay on paper.

items.headline: Cyclone Murasu hits Andhra Pradesh with winds of about 120 km/h
items.text: Cyclone Murasu made landfall in Andhra Pradesh by the early hours of 3 November. Landfall means the centre of the storm crossing from sea onto land. Winds reached about 120 km/h, and heavy rain fell as the landfall continued. Forecasters had expected it to cross near Ongole with winds of 100–110 km/h, gusting to 120 km/h. Heavy rain alerts covered five states: Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Tamil Nadu, Telangana and Chhattisgarh. Chennai and Tiruvallur closed schools and colleges on 2 November. It is not yet known how much damage the storm has caused.
items.background: A cyclone is a large rotating storm that forms over warm sea and brings strong winds and heavy rain.
items.why: If you live in any of the five alert states, expect heavy rain; Chennai and Tiruvallur have already shut schools.

items.headline: Delhi air turns 'very poor' as GRAP Stage 2 curbs begin
items.text: Delhi-NCR moved to GRAP Stage 2 on 2 November. Delhi's average air quality index (AQI, a 0–500 pollution score) rose from 117 on 31 October to 324 on 2 November. That is almost three times worse in two days. On 3 November the R K Puram station read 374. Rohini (429), Punjabi Bagh (424) and Bawana (408) were in the 'severe' band. Stage 2 bans coal and firewood, including tandoors. Diesel generators are allowed only for emergencies. Roads get mechanical sweeping and water sprinkling, with tighter dust checks at building sites. The Supreme Court has allowed certified green firecrackers for two days around Diwali on 8 November.
items.background: GRAP, the Graded Response Action Plan, is a ladder of pollution curbs for Delhi-NCR. Each stage adds stricter rules as air gets worse.
items.why: Separately, the health ministry has told states to record pollution-linked illness with standard disease codes and follow up high-risk patients.

items.headline: TRAI orders telecom networks to link up over internet technology
items.text: TRAI, India's telecom regulator, has made IP-based interconnection compulsory from January 2027. Interconnection is how one operator's network hands a call to another's. An example is a Jio user calling an Airtel user. IP-based means calls pass between networks as internet-style data packets, not over older circuit-switched links. The new interconnection rules take effect from January 2027. The reports give no details yet on any change to tariffs or call quality for users. There is no direct effect on your bill reported so far.
items.background: Calls between different telecom companies must cross from one network into another. The technology used at that hand-over point is what TRAI is changing.
items.why: This changes how every call between two operators is passed along, although no direct effect on users has been reported.

items.headline: NEET-UG 2027 likely to stay on paper, reports say
items.text: NEET-UG, the national entrance exam for medical colleges, will probably stay a pen-and-paper test in 2027, Medical Dialogues reported on 3 November. The move to a computer-based test (CBT), where students answer on screens at test centres, may wait until 2028. Shiksha.com reports that southern states oppose the full online shift. These are media reports, not an official announcement. Separately, the Staff Selection Commission (SSC) has published its November 2026 exam dates. They cover CGEPT, departmental tests and Delhi Police SI Paper-II.
items.background: NEET-UG decides admission to medical seats across India. Any change in its format affects how lakhs of students prepare.
items.why: Students preparing for NEET-UG 2027 should, for now, plan for a paper exam until official word comes.

sections.title: Markets & money
sections.gist: Rate rises spread as Australia hits an 18-year high. Tech worries hit Asian stocks, and the RBI surveys households before December.

items.headline: Marvell agrees to buy Lumentum for $115 billion in shares
items.text: On 2 November US chipmaker Marvell Technology agreed to buy Lumentum in a deal valued at $115 billion. It is an all-stock deal. That means Lumentum's owners will be paid in Marvell shares, not cash. The two companies say the merger will create a 'category leader' in AI connectivity. AI connectivity means the parts that move data between computers inside AI data centres. Shareholders still have to approve the deal. It is expected to close in the first half of 2028, so the merger would take more than a year to complete.
items.background: AI systems run on thousands of chips that must constantly share data. Firms making the links between those chips have become valuable.
items.why: The size of the deal shows how much money is still going into AI data-centre hardware, even as investors question that spending.

items.headline: Oracle seeks $20 billion for AI build-out as Asian stocks slip
items.text: Oracle filed on 2 November to sell $20 billion of new shares and bonds to pay for its AI build-out. Half of that, $10 billion, is high-grade dollar bonds. High-grade bonds are loans from investors to a company seen as very likely to repay. Selling new shares means existing owners each hold a smaller slice of the company. On 3 November, Asian stocks fell ahead of the US midterm elections as worries about tech companies weighed on markets. Oil prices held steady. What to watch: how US markets react to the midterm results.
items.background: Big tech companies are spending huge sums on AI computing, and investors are questioning whether that spending will pay off.
items.why: Oracle needing to raise $20 billion shows how costly the AI race is, and tech worries are moving Asian markets.

items.headline: Australia raises interest rates to highest level since 2008
items.text: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its main interest rate, the cash rate, by 25 basis points to 4.85% on 3 November. A basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point, so 25 basis points is 0.25 points. It was the bank's fifth rate hike of 2026. The rate is now at its highest level since 2008, an 18-year high. The Australian dollar fell after the decision. In Europe, Bundesbank president Joachim Nagel said the European Central Bank will probably have to raise rates in December.
items.background: Central banks raise interest rates to make borrowing costlier, which slows spending and helps bring prices down.
items.why: Major central banks are still raising borrowing costs, a sign that inflation remains a problem in several big economies.

items.headline: RBI launches surveys on inflation expectations before December meeting
items.text: The RBI, India's central bank, launched three surveys on 3 November. They will measure what people expect prices to do and how confident consumers feel. The results will feed into the RBI's December policy meeting. Separately, on 3 November India eased foreign-exchange reporting rules for small-value exports and imports of services. These are the rules on how businesses report money coming in from, or going out to, other countries. What to watch: the RBI's December decision.
items.background: The RBI sets the repo rate, the rate at which it lends to banks, at its policy meetings.
items.why: The repo rate guides what banks charge on loans, so the December meeting matters for anyone borrowing.

items.headline: SBI profit up 14.3%; NSE up 23% in first listed results
items.text: On 3 November State Bank of India (SBI) reported a net profit of ₹23,038 crore for July–September, up 14.3% from a year earlier. Part of the rise came from an exceptional gain, a one-off item that will not repeat every quarter. Net interest income, the gap between interest earned on loans and interest paid on deposits, beat analysts' estimates. SBI says it aims for a net interest margin above 3%. NSE, India's largest stock exchange, posted its first results as a listed company. Its consolidated net profit rose 23% to ₹2,578 crore, helped by higher trading volumes.
items.background: Q2 means July–September 2026, the second quarter of India's financial year. SBI is India's biggest bank and NSE recently listed its own shares.
items.why: SBI's margins show how bank lending profits are holding up as rates rise. NSE's profit reflects how actively Indians are trading.

sections.title: Tech & AI
sections.gist: Google shuts down a 1.3-million-device botnet hidden in TV-box firmware and bans the Chinese maker it blames.

items.headline: Google shuts down 1.3-million-device Android TV box botnet
items.text: On 2 November Google said it had dismantled XCPE, a botnet of more than 1.3 million Android TV streaming boxes. A botnet is a crowd of hijacked devices that criminals control remotely. The malware was built into the boxes' firmware, the core software, at the factory. Google says, with high confidence, that Chinese maker Videostrong Technology Co. deliberately built and ran the backdoor for profit. Google revoked Videostrong's licence to make Android TV devices with Google apps and banned it and future affiliates. It also took down the control servers. Removing the malware does not work, because it reinstalls itself. Owners need clean firmware or should disconnect the box from the internet.
items.background: Cheap streaming boxes often run Android. Uncertified ones can come with hidden software that owners cannot see or remove.
items.why: If you use a cheap Android TV box, it may be infected from the factory, and deleting apps will not fix it.

sections.title: Formula 1
sections.gist: Kimi Antonelli becomes F1's youngest-ever champion in Mexico, while Haas drops Ocon and hands Rafa Camara a home debut in Brazil.

items.headline: Kimi Antonelli becomes youngest F1 world champion in history
items.text: Kimi Antonelli was crowned the 2026 Formula 1 world champion at the Mexico City Grand Prix. He won the title without winning the race. Max Verstappen won in Mexico City, with Lewis Hamilton second. Antonelli is now the youngest driver ever to win the F1 World Championship. He already held another age record as F1's youngest pole-sitter, the driver who starts first after qualifying. He was also the first driver to turn his first three pole positions into race wins.
items.background: The F1 world championship goes to the driver with the most points across a season's races, so it can be clinched without winning.
items.why: A new record holder for youngest champion marks a handover to a new generation in the sport.

items.headline: Haas drops Ocon for rest of 2026; Camara debuts in Brazil
items.text: Haas said on 3 November that Esteban Ocon will no longer race for the team in the 2026 championship. He had already been dropped for the Mexico Grand Prix after a row. Autosport reports that relations had been strained, and a heated argument in Mexico was the final straw. Rafa Camara, a Ferrari junior driver who leads F2, the series below F1, will replace him. Camara was already signed to take Ocon's seat in 2027. He will now make his F1 debut early, at his home Sao Paulo Grand Prix, alongside Oliver Bearman. Haas has still not confirmed Bearman for 2027.
items.background: Haas is a smaller F1 team that works closely with Ferrari and often runs Ferrari's young drivers.
items.why: A team fight has handed a young driver his F1 debut early, and in front of his home crowd.

sections.title: Cricket — the masala
sections.gist: Reports say Mumbai and Punjab are near a Hardik Pandya–Arshdeep Singh swap; concussed Devon Conway misses New Zealand's first ODI against India.

items.headline: Reports: Mumbai and Punjab near Hardik Pandya–Arshdeep Singh swap
items.text: Mumbai Indians and Punjab Kings are reported to be close to swapping Hardik Pandya and Arshdeep Singh before IPL 2027. NDTV reported on 3 November that the two teams are closing in on the deal. Sportstar, calling it an exclusive, says the trade taking Pandya to Punjab is nearing completion. Neither team has confirmed it. Pandya returned to Mumbai in an all-cash trade from Gujarat Titans before IPL 2024. The Hindu notes his three seasons as Mumbai captain since then brought little success. A swap would bring Mumbai a frontline India pace bowler and give Punjab Pandya.
items.background: IPL teams can trade players directly, outside the auction. A swap exchanges players; an all-cash trade means one team simply pays for a player.
items.why: Two India stars changing franchises would reshape both teams and Mumbai's captaincy plans before IPL 2027.

items.headline: Devon Conway concussed, misses New Zealand's first ODI against India
items.text: New Zealand opener Devon Conway will miss the first one-day international (ODI) against India. He collided with his teammate, fast bowler Matt Henry, and took a blow to the head. New Zealand Cricket (NZC) said he was taken to a hospital emergency department for checks. Those checks confirmed a concussion, a brain injury caused by a knock to the head. Losing a first-choice opener forces New Zealand to reshuffle their top order for the series opener. NZC has not said when Conway could return.
items.background: Concussion rules in cricket stop a player from playing until doctors clear them, because a second blow soon after can be dangerous.
items.why: It weakens New Zealand's batting for the first match of their ODI series against India.

quiz.q: Suppose Democrats win both chambers but fall short of two-thirds. Trump vetoes their bill. What happens?
options: The bill becomes law anyway, because Democrats hold both chambers
The bill dies unless two-thirds of both chambers vote to override
The Vice President casts a vote to decide it
quiz.why: A simple majority can pass a bill, but overruling a veto needs two-thirds of both the House and the Senate.

quiz.q: Why can India's 15 July order lower the risk to Indian seafarers but not remove it?
options: It covers only ships crossing Hormuz, but vessels sailing nearby can still be attacked
It applies only to foreign sailors working on Indian ships
It was cancelled before the attack on 2 November
quiz.why: The order keeps Indian crews off ships crossing Hormuz. It cannot stop attacks on vessels near the strait, such as Al Jusufi off Musandam.

quiz.q: In April–June 2026, India bought fewer tonnes of gold, yet the rupee value hit a record. How?
options: Prices rose enough that fewer grams still cost more rupees in total
Families bought more grams of gold than a year before
The government cut import duties, making gold cheaper
quiz.why: Grams equal budget divided by price. A big enough price rise means fewer grams can still add up to more rupees.
